subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Made Disha's Uttapam Go Bad?
periods.textbook_anchor: Food Spoilage — Students share experiences of upset stomachs and spoiled food, then write why they think food gets spoiled (p. 42)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening story of detective Disha finding her three-day-old uttapam covered in coloured patches and emitting a foul smell. Students are invited to share a time they encountered spoiled food — what it looked like, smelled like, and what happened when someone ate it. The class pools these experiences on the board as a quick word-cloud (smell, colour, texture, upset stomach).

The teacher guides a focused discussion using Textbook p. 42: Have you ever had an upset stomach — what could have caused it? What might happen if spoiled food is eaten by mistake? Students discuss in pairs, then share with the class. The teacher introduces the word 'microbe' as Aditya explains it in the story — tiny living organisms that exist everywhere and are responsible for the patches and smell. Students note the key idea: microbes need moisture, air, and the right temperature to grow.

Students independently write their response to Textbook p. 42: Why do you think food gets spoiled? They may use the discussion points and the idea of microbes. The teacher circulates, prompting those who finish quickly to think of one food that spoils quickly and one that lasts longer, and to speculate why.

Selected students read their written responses aloud. The class compares ideas — were they all about microbes, or did some mention heat, air, or water? The teacher closes by posing an open question: if microbes need moisture, air, and warmth, what might we do to stop them? This question is left open for the class to carry forward as curiousity, not as a promised next topic.

periods.implied_lo: Students can draw on personal and textbook experience to propose a reasoned explanation for why a natural process (spoilage) occurs under certain conditions.
periods.section_context: Detective Disha's forgotten uttapam, mould patches, foul smell, microbes as tiny living organisms, upset stomach from spoiled food, conditions needed by microbes (moisture, air, temperature).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of these foods — bread, pickle, or dry chilli powder — do you think would last longest at home, and why?' This surfaces children's implicit knowledge of preservation even before the section is named, and gently draws out traditional household wisdom about keeping food safe.

periods.activity_title: Sun, Salt, and Oil — Drying and Preservation at Home
periods.textbook_anchor: Food Preservation — Students place tomato slices on a sunlit surface and observe changes, connecting drying to preservation (p. 45)
materials: One small tomato per group (or one shared per two groups)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of chillies drying in the sun (p. 44 area)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly links back to the idea that microbes need moisture to grow — established when the class discussed Disha's uttapam. Today's question: can we remove that moisture? Students look at Textbook p. 45 together. The teacher slices the tomatoes (or has them pre-sliced for hygiene) and each group places their slices on a tray or plate to be set on the windowsill in sunlight. Students predict in their notebooks: what will change about the tomato slice by the end of the unit?

While the slices sit in sunlight, students work from Textbook p. 44: they write the names of other things that are dried to remain unspoilt throughout the year, and list items that can be made from mangoes to enjoy them for longer. The teacher circulates and encourages students to think of what their own families dry at home — chillies, fish, papad, amla — connecting the textbook examples to lived experience.

Students return to their tomato slices and record their observations — any change in surface, firmness, or size — in their notebooks. They then discuss in groups: what is the drying process actually removing, and how does that connect to microbes? The teacher draws the link to oil in pickles (Textbook p. 45): what would happen if no oil were added to the pickle — would air reach the mango? Students discuss this question from Textbook p. 45.

Groups share their tomato observations and their answers to the pickle-oil question. The teacher summarises the two preservation ideas explored — drying to remove moisture, and oiling to block air — and asks: which of these methods have you seen someone in your family use? Students note one family preservation practice they know of, as a prompt toward the inquiry from Textbook p. 46.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple observation-based investigation to link a physical change (moisture loss) to a condition that controls microbial growth.
periods.section_context: Tomato slices in sunlight, chilli drying to make chilli powder, mango products, mustard oil poured over pickled mangoes, moisture removal, air blockage, Textbook p. 44 and p. 45 tasks.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students list things their families dry, ask: 'Does anyone's family dry fish, or amla, or papad? Who taught them to do this?' This surfaces inherited preservation knowledge and opens the idea that these methods have been used for generations across India.

periods.activity_title: Family Secrets — Finding Out How Elders Preserve Food
periods.textbook_anchor: Food Preservation — Students find out and write at least one food preservation practice from their family by asking elders at home (p. 46)
materials: Optional: index cards for displaying findings

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking: refrigerators are a recent invention — how did families keep food safe before them? Students brainstorm briefly. The teacher then introduces the task from Textbook p. 46: each student will think of one food preservation practice they know from their own family or community — a method an elder at home uses or has described. For students who have already asked elders before coming to class, they share now; for those who have not, the teacher invites them to draw on anything they have observed at home.

Students write their family preservation practice in their notebooks in the style of Disha's detective findings — 'Finding #[number]: In my family, we preserve [food] by [method] because…' They are encouraged to name the food, the method (salt, sun, oil, spices, cold, fermentation), and what they think the method is doing. The teacher circulates and helps students who are stuck by asking: 'Have you ever seen anyone at home make pickle, or dry something on the roof, or store something in a clay pot?'

Students share their findings in a gallery format — they read their detective entries aloud or display them on the board if index cards are used. The class notices patterns: which methods appear most often? Are any methods unique to a region or community? The teacher notes methods on the board in four columns: Drying, Salting/Spicing, Oiling/Pickling, Cold/Other, without privileging any one.

The teacher draws together the range of methods and highlights that different families and regions across India have developed these practices over centuries, all aiming at the same goal — controlling moisture, air, or temperature to slow microbes. The class reflects briefly: what does this variety of methods tell us about how people have solved the same problem in different ways?

periods.implied_lo: Students can gather information from a community source, record it systematically, and connect it to a scientific explanation they have constructed.
periods.section_context: Family and community food preservation practices, drying, salting, oiling, pickling, spicing, fermentation (idli batter), methods used for centuries in India, Textbook p. 46 task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone's family mention a reason WHY a particular method works — like salt drawing out water, or oil keeping air away?' Connecting elders' practical explanations to the science vocabulary the class has built honours both kinds of knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Market Eyes — Observing How Elders Choose Fresh Food
periods.textbook_anchor: My Food, My Pride — Students observe how elders select fruits and vegetables in the market and write one learning as a detective finding (p. 49)
materials: Optional: a few sample vegetables or fruits brought to class (e.g. one ripe and one overripe tomato, one fresh and one wilted spinach bunch)

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the scene: Disha visits the vegetable market with her Thatha and notices how carefully elders choose fresh produce. The teacher asks: when you go to the market, do you notice how an elder picks a vegetable — do they press it, smell it, look at the colour? Students share observations from their own experience. If sample produce is available, the teacher holds up the contrasting pair and asks students to describe what they see and feel.

Students open Textbook p. 49 and read the task about the market observation activity. Working individually, they write their 'Finding #9' in their notebooks — one clear observation they have made (or would make) about how an elder selects fresh vegetables or fruit. The teacher circulates, prompting specificity: not just 'they look at the colour' but 'Thatha pressed the tomato — a fresh one is firm, a spoiled one is soft.' Students who have not visited a market are encouraged to think of what they have seen in their home kitchen when produce is checked.

Several students read their finding aloud. The class builds a shared list on the board: visual cues (colour, shine, absence of dark spots), tactile cues (firmness, not slimy), smell cues. The teacher asks: why might a seasonal, locally grown fruit need fewer such checks than one that has travelled far? This introduces the concept from the section that local and seasonal food is fresher because it travels a shorter distance.

Students note from Textbook p. 50 three seasonal fruits or vegetables of their own region as the section invites. The teacher facilitates a brief sharing: which are summer fruits? Which are winter vegetables? The observation closes with a reflection: how does choosing seasonal produce connect to what the class has been learning about freshness and spoilage?

periods.implied_lo: Students can use structured observation to identify quality indicators in everyday objects, and connect those indicators to an underlying natural process.
periods.section_context: Disha's market visit with Thatha, elder selection of fresh produce, visual and tactile checks for freshness, seasonal fruits (lychee, amla, jamun), local and seasonal food, Textbook p. 49 and p. 50 tasks.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone's grandparent or elder ever told them a rule for picking the best mango or choosing the freshest fish at the market?' Regional selection wisdom varies and all answers are valid — celebrate diversity of practice rather than converging on one correct method.

periods.activity_title: Teeth at Work — Exploring the Mouth's First Step in Digestion
periods.textbook_anchor: Chew Right! — Students chew food carefully, identify which teeth they used, and name them from the diagram (p. 50)
materials: A small piece of bread or a biscuit per student (or a clean cracker)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of teeth types (p. 51 area) — incisors, canines, premolars, molars

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: do you ever think about what is happening inside your mouth while you eat? Students share briefly. The teacher introduces the task from Textbook p. 50: students will chew a small piece of bread very slowly and deliberately, paying attention to which teeth are doing which job. Each student receives a small piece of bread or cracker.

Students chew their piece of food slowly, as instructed in Textbook p. 50 — chewing until the food becomes mush. The teacher asks them to pause and notice: which teeth did the first bite (the front teeth)? Which teeth are grinding the food now (the back teeth)? Students record their observations in their notebooks — a rough sketch of their mouth with labels showing where the action happened.

Students open to the teeth diagram in the textbook. Together, the class names each tooth type from the diagram: incisors (cut), canines (tear), premolars (crush), molars (grind). Students match their chewing experience to the diagram — which teeth did which job in their observation? They write a short explanation in their notebooks linking each tooth name to its function and to what they felt.

The teacher asks: besides the teeth, did anyone notice something wet helping to soften the food? Students identify saliva and the teacher explains its role in digestion — saliva mixes with the food and begins breaking it down. Students read the brief Textbook p. 50 passage on saliva, then write their answer to Textbook p. 53 on how to avoid choking, connecting it to the idea of chewing properly before swallowing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can match the structural features of a body part to its function by observing that part performing a task on a familiar material.
periods.section_context: Incisors, canines, premolars, molars, their cutting/tearing/crushing/grinding functions, saliva's role in digestion, proper chewing, avoiding choking, Textbook p. 50 and p. 53 tasks.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What happens when you eat very fast and swallow big pieces — have you ever felt uncomfortable?' This connects the anatomy lesson directly to safe eating behaviour and oral hygiene without needing to be prescriptive about it.

periods.activity_title: Brushing Up — Oral Hygiene as Daily Practice
periods.textbook_anchor: Chew Right! — Students describe how to avoid choking and reflect on safe eating and oral hygiene habits (p. 53)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a question: after you eat, what do you do for your teeth and mouth? Students share their routines. The teacher lists practices named on the board without evaluating them yet — rinse, brush, chew gum, nothing. This surfaces what students actually do and creates a safe space for honest sharing.

The class revisits Textbook p. 53 together. Students read about oral hygiene — rinsing the mouth after eating, brushing regularly, and visiting a dentist. They also re-read the safe-eating points: smaller mouthfuls, proper chewing, not gulping food. Students write in their notebooks a personal hygiene plan: three things they will commit to doing to keep their mouth and teeth healthy, written in the first person ('I will...').

In pairs, students role-play a short conversation: one student is eating quickly and gulping food; the other gently explains what is happening inside the mouth and what the risks are. Each pair performs for about one minute. The teacher circulates and listens for correct use of vocabulary (teeth names, saliva, choking) and for the tone being caring rather than scolding.

The class reconvenes. The teacher returns to the board list from the opening and asks: which practices do we want to keep, add, or reconsider? The list is revised collaboratively. The teacher closes by noting that caring for teeth is a lifelong habit — the class has used both the anatomy they explored earlier and today's reflection to understand why the habit matters.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate a safe personal behaviour, explain the reasoning behind it using biological knowledge, and practise communicating it to a peer.
periods.section_context: Oral hygiene routines (rinsing, brushing, dental check-ups), safe eating behaviour (smaller mouthfuls, chewing properly, avoiding choking), role-play of safe eating conversation, Textbook p. 53 task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students share that they do not have access to a toothbrush, respond with sensitivity and ask: 'What do people use when a toothbrush is not available — has anyone's family used neem twigs or charcoal?' This opens discussion of traditional oral care without singling anyone out.

periods.activity_title: Good Microbe, Bad Microbe — Closing Disha's Detective Notebook
periods.textbook_anchor: Food in Our Body — Students discuss why some foods last weeks while others spoil in days, and plan food for a two-day field trip (p. 53)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reopens the mystery that launched the chapter: Disha found mould on her uttapam, and the chapter has been tracking why. Now the class has one more layer to add — microbes are not only harmful. The teacher asks: does anyone know of a food that is made WITH the help of tiny living things? Students guess; the teacher introduces fermentation through idli batter rising and curd forming, as described in this section.

Students read the relevant passage from this section and discuss in small groups the dual role of microbes: some spoil food and make us ill, while others help make food (idli, curd) and aid digestion in the stomach. Groups then tackle the discussion question from Textbook p. 53: why do some food items last for weeks while others spoil in just a few days? Each group prepares a two-sentence answer that must mention at least one condition microbes need.

Groups share their answers. The teacher then poses the field-trip planning task from Textbook p. 53: you are going on a field trip for two days — list five food items you will carry and explain how you will keep them from spoiling. Students write this individually in their notebooks, choosing foods and preservation strategies from what the class has discussed across the chapter. Emphasis is on reasoning: not just what to pack, but why each item will stay safe.

The teacher invites students to imagine a world without food preservation (Textbook p. 53 discussion prompt) — what would families eat? What would happen to food systems? Students share one consequence each. The teacher closes by returning to the matching activity from Textbook p. 54: students draw lines matching food items to preservation methods and final products, consolidating the full range of methods covered in the chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of microbial conditions to evaluate food choices and preservation strategies in a practical scenario.
periods.section_context: Dual role of microbes (spoilage vs. fermentation/digestion), idli batter fermentation, curd, field-trip food planning, preservation method matching activity, world-without-preservation scenario, Textbook p. 53 and p. 54 tasks.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the field-trip task, ask: 'Would your answer change if the trip were in summer rather than winter — why?' This pushes students to think about temperature as a variable and surfaces the role of seasonal context in preservation decisions.

periods.activity_title: Disha's Final Case File — A Whole-Chapter Exhibition
periods.textbook_anchor: Food in Our Body — Students match food items, preservation methods, and final products, synthesising the chapter's key ideas (p. 54)

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the task: each student will create a single-page 'Case File' for detective Disha that brings together everything the chapter has uncovered. The case file has four sections — what spoils food and why (microbes and their conditions), how we preserve food (at least three methods with examples), how the mouth helps us eat safely (teeth types, saliva, oral hygiene), and one example of a good microbe. Students plan their four sections in a rough layout before writing.

Students create their case file pages — written, drawn, or a combination — working individually on plain paper or in their notebooks. The teacher circulates and encourages students to use the vocabulary and examples from across the chapter: microbes, moisture, fermentation, incisors, saliva, pickling, drying, seasonal food. Students who finish early are invited to add a 'Detective's Recommendation' section advising how to eat and store food wisely.

Students share their case files in a gallery walk — pages displayed on desks, students moving around and reading one another's work. They leave a small tick or star on any case file that includes an idea they had not thought of themselves. The teacher joins the gallery walk, noting strong examples of reasoning to highlight in the close.

The teacher gathers the class and reads out two or three ideas noticed in the gallery — without naming authors unless students volunteer — that particularly well connected a scientific idea to a cultural practice, or that showed original reasoning. The teacher closes by reflecting that Disha's mystery turned out to be about a world invisible to the naked eye, yet connected to every meal, every preservation tradition, and every tooth in our mouth.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise concepts from natural science and cultural practice across a chapter to produce a coherent, evidence-based explanatory account.
periods.section_context: Microbes and spoilage conditions, food preservation methods (drying, pickling, oiling, salting, refrigeration, canning), good microbes (fermentation, digestion), teeth types and functions, saliva, oral hygiene, seasonal and local food, matching activity from Textbook p. 54.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: During the gallery walk, look for case files that bridge the natural and cultural strands — for example, a student who connects sun-drying to removing moisture for microbes AND to a family tradition. Use these as examples in the close to show the class how science and culture explain each other.

assessment_items.question_text: Disha left her uttapam on the kitchen counter for three days. It developed coloured patches and smelled bad. What caused the uttapam to spoil?

options.label: A
options.text: The colour patches appeared because the uttapam absorbed dust from the air around it.

options.label: B
options.text: The uttapam became stale because it was left uncovered and lost its taste naturally over time.

options.label: C
options.text: The uttapam was cooked incorrectly and the wrong ingredients caused the colour to change.

options.label: D
options.text: Tiny living organisms called microbes grew on the uttapam using the moisture, air, and warmth available.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether the student can name microbes and link their growth to specific environmental conditions (moisture, air, temperature) rather than attributing spoilage to vague or unscientific causes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can draw on personal and textbook experience to propose a reasoned explanation for why a natural process (spoilage) occurs under certain conditions.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this indicates the student holds a vague 'staleness' model of spoilage and has not connected the process to living organisms and their growth conditions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this suggests the student attributes spoilage to cooking error rather than to microbial action — a common conflation of food quality with food safety.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting this shows the student may associate visible particles (dust) with the patches rather than understanding that microbes are living organisms too small to see with the naked eye.

assessment_items.question_text: A student placed tomato slices on a tray in a sunny window and checked them after several hours. She noticed the slices had become smaller, drier, and slightly wrinkled. Explain what happened to the tomato slices and how this process helps preserve food.
expected_elements: The sunlight caused moisture (water) in the tomato slices to evaporate, reducing the water content of the slices.
Microbes need moisture to grow; removing moisture slows or stops microbial growth.
Dried tomato slices therefore last longer without spoiling because the condition microbes need (moisture) has been removed.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for a response that names moisture loss, connects moisture to microbial growth conditions, and concludes that removal of moisture slows spoilage. Partial credit if two of the three elements are present. Regional examples of sun-drying (fish, chillies, papad, amla) are equally acceptable as supporting examples.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple observation-based investigation to link a physical change (moisture loss) to a condition that controls microbial growth.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Sunlight caused water/moisture in the tomato to evaporate, making the slice smaller and drier.
Microbes need moisture to grow; without it, their growth is slowed or prevented.
This is why drying is a preservation method — it removes the condition microbes need, so the food lasts longer.

assessment_items.task: Think of one food preservation practice that someone in your family or community uses — for example, making pickle, drying something in the sun, adding lots of salt or spices, or keeping food in a cool place. Write about this practice as a detective finding: name the food, describe the method, and explain what you think the method is doing to keep the food safe from microbes.
assessment_items.scaffold: My Finding: In my family/community, we preserve [name the food] by [describe the method]. I think this works because [explain what the method does to moisture, air, or temperature that slows microbes].
format_of_output: A written detective finding of three to five sentences
Must name a specific food and a specific method
Must include a reason connecting the method to what microbes need
assessment_items.annotation: All regionally varied preservation practices are acceptable and correct — pickling with mustard oil, drying fish or amla, making jam with sugar, storing in clay pots, making papads, fermenting rice. The scientific reasoning (what the method does to moisture, air, or temperature) is the key marking criterion, not the choice of food or method. Accept oral traditions and elder-transmitted knowledge as valid sources.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather information from a community source, record it systematically, and connect it to a scientific explanation they have constructed.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can identify a cultural food practice from their community, describe it accurately, and explain it using the scientific framework of microbial conditions (moisture, air, temperature) built during the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides the student through three moves: name the food, describe the method, explain the mechanism. A response that skips the explanation and only names food and method is incomplete — the scientific connection is the key element.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific food and method, explains the mechanism clearly (e.g. 'oil covers the mango so air cannot reach it, and without air the microbes cannot grow'). Weak: names a food and method but gives no mechanism, or repeats the method without explaining why it works.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students without direct access to a market or kitchen preservation tradition may write about a practice they have heard described, seen in a picture book or video, or observed at a neighbour's or relative's home. All sources of knowledge — grandparents, community elders, media — are valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written detective finding (prose, three to five sentences)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The detective-finding format matches the chapter's narrative frame and encourages students to present reasoning as an organised conclusion rather than a list, supporting analytical writing development.

assessment_items.question_text: Disha's Thatha pressed a tomato gently before buying it at the market. Which of the following best explains why checking the firmness of a tomato helps judge its freshness?

options.label: A
options.text: A firm tomato has not yet lost moisture and has not been broken down by microbial action, so it is less likely to have begun spoiling.

options.label: B
options.text: A firm tomato is always red, and red tomatoes are tastier than green ones.

options.label: C
options.text: Pressing a tomato shows how long it was stored in the refrigerator before reaching the market.

options.label: D
options.text: Soft tomatoes have more seeds, which means they are overripe and no longer nutritious.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item links the market-observation skill to the scientific concept of microbial spoilage, testing whether the student can connect a sensory quality indicator (firmness) to the underlying biological process (moisture loss and microbial breakdown).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use structured observation to identify quality indicators in everyday objects, and connect those indicators to an underlying natural process.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this shows the student conflates colour with freshness and taste, a common lay association, without connecting to the scientific concept of spoilage or microbial action.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this indicates a misconception that firmness is a marker of refrigeration history rather than of microbial breakdown — the student has not linked tactile observation to the biological process.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this reveals a confusion between ripeness (seeds) and nutritional value, showing the student has not connected firmness as a freshness indicator to microbial action and moisture loss.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the diagram of teeth in your textbook. A student bites into an apple and then chews it into mush before swallowing. Name the teeth used at each stage and explain what each type does.
expected_elements: Incisors (front teeth) are used to cut or bite off a piece of the apple.
Canines may be used to tear the piece if needed.
Premolars crush the apple piece into smaller bits.
Molars grind the apple into a soft mush ready for swallowing.
Saliva mixes with the food during chewing and helps begin digestion.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for correctly naming all four tooth types with their functions in sequence. Award partial credit for three correct pairings. Saliva's role is a bonus element — accept it if present but do not penalise its absence if all four tooth types are correctly described.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can match the structural features of a body part to its function by observing that part performing a task on a familiar material.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: Incisors: front teeth used to cut or bite off a piece of food.
Canines: pointed teeth used to tear food.
Premolars: used to crush food into smaller pieces.
Molars: broad back teeth used to grind food into a soft mush.
(Bonus) Saliva mixes with the chewed food and begins the digestion process.

assessment_items.task: Think about what you have learned about keeping your mouth and teeth healthy. Write three things you will do every day to protect your teeth and eat safely. For each thing, write one sentence explaining WHY it helps — using what you know about teeth, saliva, or the risk of choking.
assessment_items.scaffold:
1. I will [habit]. This helps because [reason linked to teeth/saliva/safety].
2. I will [habit]. This helps because [reason].
3. I will [habit]. This helps because [reason].
format_of_output: Three written commitments, each with a linked reason
Each reason must connect to biological knowledge (teeth function, saliva, choking prevention)
assessment_items.annotation: Mark for the quality of reasoning, not for the choice of habit. A student who writes 'I will brush twice a day because teeth collect food particles that can be broken down by bacteria and cause decay' shows stronger reasoning than one who writes 'I will brush because it keeps teeth clean.' All culturally valid oral hygiene practices (neem twigs, charcoal, oil-pulling) are acceptable if the student provides a reasoning sentence.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate a safe personal behaviour, explain the reasoning behind it using biological knowledge, and practise communicating it to a peer.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of precaution, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate biological knowledge about teeth and oral safety into a personal action plan with explained reasoning, showing the link between understanding and behaviour.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each numbered line demands two things: a habit and a reason. A response that lists three habits without reasons meets only half the task. The reasoning sentence is what distinguishes this item from a simple recall list.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: each reason is specific and uses biological vocabulary (e.g. saliva, enamel, choking, microbes). Weak: reasons are generic ('it is good for health') without connecting to the body's mechanisms. Partial: habits are named and some reasons given but the biological connection is vague.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may name any culturally familiar oral hygiene practice — neem twigs, miswak, charcoal powder, oil rinsing — as long as they explain a reason. The goal is reasoning, not conformity to a single practice. Students who struggle with writing may draw the three habits with a label and a reason note beside each drawing.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written personal action plan (three items with reasons)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The first-person commitment format mirrors the personal hygiene plan students wrote during the unit and reinforces the idea that biological knowledge should translate into practised behaviour.

assessment_items.question_text: You are packing food for a two-day summer field trip with no refrigerator available. Choose three food items you would carry and explain, for each one, how you would keep it from spoiling during the trip. Use what you know about what microbes need to grow.
look_for: The student names three specific food items (not generic categories) appropriate for a field trip.
For each food item, the student describes a specific preservation or storage strategy (e.g. sealed container, salted, dried, oiled, kept in shade).
Each strategy is linked to at least one microbial condition it addresses: removing moisture, blocking air, keeping temperature low, or using salt/spice/oil.
The student shows awareness that summer heat is a relevant variable affecting microbe growth speed.
The overall response is coherent — the three choices together form a practical, feasible field-trip food plan.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative reasoning task. Award highest marks for responses that correctly apply microbial-condition logic to realistic food choices and storage strategies, not for naming the 'correct' foods. Regional food choices (poha, flattened rice, murmure, chikki, dried fish, roasted gram) are all acceptable. The explanatory quality of the reasoning is the marking criterion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of microbial conditions to evaluate food choices and preservation strategies in a practical scenario.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

look_for: Three named food items with individual strategies — not a single strategy applied generically to all three.
Each strategy correctly identifies at least one microbial condition it addresses (moisture, air, temperature, salt/acid/oil).
Summer heat is mentioned as a factor that accelerates microbial growth, raising the stakes of the preservation choices.
The food choices are realistic and culturally appropriate — the student is applying knowledge, not reciting a textbook list.
The response is structured and legible — ideas are sequenced clearly even if not in formal paragraphs.

assessment_items.question_text: Microbes are often thought of as harmful because they spoil food and cause illness. But the chapter shows that microbes also play helpful roles. Using examples from the chapter, explain TWO ways microbes help us and TWO ways microbes harm us. Then explain what this means for how we should think about microbes.
look_for: Two correctly identified harmful roles: spoiling food (causing mould, foul smell, illness from eating spoiled food) and causing upset stomach or indigestion when food is contaminated.
Two correctly identified helpful roles: fermentation of idli batter (making it rise) and supporting digestion in the stomach (good microbes in curd and buttermilk).
A concluding statement that shows nuanced thinking: microbes are neither simply good nor simply bad — their role depends on the type of microbe and the context.
The response uses specific examples from the chapter rather than general statements.
The language is organised — harmful and helpful roles are clearly distinguished before the concluding reflection.
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item assesses the student's ability to hold two opposing truths simultaneously and construct a nuanced conclusion — a key thinking skill developed by the chapter's detective-narrative structure. Award highest marks for responses that give specific examples AND arrive at a reasoned, non-binary conclusion about microbes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise concepts from natural science and cultural practice across a chapter to produce a coherent, evidence-based explanatory account.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

look_for: Harmful role 1: microbes cause food spoilage — mould, coloured patches, foul smell on foods like uttapam or bread.
Harmful role 2: eating food with harmful microbes causes upset stomach, indigestion, or illness.
Helpful role 1: good microbes ferment idli batter, making it rise and producing a safe, nutritious food.
Helpful role 2: good microbes in curd and buttermilk aid digestion in the stomach.

Concluding reflection: microbes are not simply good or bad — different microbes do different things, and understanding the conditions they need helps us use them wisely and protect ourselves from harmful ones.
